Algorithm

 Home Computer science
OurBigBook.com Words: 21k Articles: 159
An algorithm is a finite, precise procedure for transforming an input into an output.
Here "finite" refers to the description: a short algorithm can perform arbitrarily many steps on increasingly large inputs. Solving a computational problem additionally requires termination and the specified output on every permitted input. State assumptions explicitly: binary search requires a sorted array.
An algorithm is an idea that can have implementations in different programming languages. Its explanation should make three things visible: the permitted inputs, the rule for each step, and the meaning of the returned output. Algorithm correctness then separates finding the right answer from eventually finishing; time complexity asks how much work finishing requires.
A particularly useful design question is: what knowledge survives each step? In binary search, it is the location of every possible match inside the remaining candidate range. Writing that fact as a loop invariant turns an intuitive shortcut into a procedure whose discarded candidates can be justified. This often helps discover the algorithm, rather than merely check it afterward.

FM-index

Words: 50
String-searching algorithm OurBigBook.com
An FM-index is a compressed text index supporting backward search through the Burrows-Wheeler transform and occurrence counts. Character rank queries locate a matching interval; sampled suffix array positions then allow the actual text positions to be recovered. Query length, number of matches and the chosen sampling density control different parts of the search cost.[ref]

Backward search

Words: 48
String-searching algorithm OurBigBook.com
Backward search finds a query's matching interval in a suffix array by processing the query from right to left. With inclusive one-based interval [l,r], prepending c changes it to [C(c)+Occ(c,l−1)+1,C(c)+Occ(c,r)]. An empty interval means no match. This works through the occurrence-order property of the last-to-first mapping.[ref]

Last-to-first mapping (LF(r)=C(Lr​)+Occ(Lr​,r))

Words: 76
String-searching algorithm OurBigBook.com
In a sorted cyclic rotation matrix, the last-to-first mapping sends the kth occurrence of a character in the last column to its kth occurrence in the first column. For one-based rows, LF(r)=C(Lr​)+Occ(Lr​,r), where C(c) counts smaller characters and Occ(c,r) counts c in the first r entries of the last column. It moves a rotation's start one character backwards cyclically. Equal characters retain the lexicographic order of their following sequences, which proves the occurrence-order rule.[ref]

Burrows-Wheeler transform (BWT(S))

Words: 56
String-searching algorithm OurBigBook.com
The Burrows-Wheeler transform appends a unique smallest terminator to a string, sorts its cyclic rotations in lexicographic order, and records the last column. It is reversible because the first and last columns contain the same characters and the last-to-first mapping preserves the occurrence order of each character. The resulting letter arrangement supports both compression and backward search.[ref]

Cycle detection

Words: 72 Articles: 1
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Determine whether repeated deterministic updates revisit a state, and optionally find the preperiod and cycle length. Recording all visited states uses memory proportional to the visited orbit. Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm detects repetition with constant extra memory.

Brent cycle-finding algorithm

Words: 39
Cycle detection OurBigBook.com
A constant-memory algorithm for detecting the eventual cycle in a sequence generated by repeated function evaluation. It holds a checkpoint fixed while a second pointer advances, doubling the checkpoint interval when exhausted; a second pass locates the start of the cycle.

Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm

Words: 63
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
For a deterministic iteration xn+1​=f(xn​) on a finite set, move one pointer by one step and another by two steps. They eventually meet inside the repeated cycle. Restarting one pointer at the initial state and advancing both by one step locates the cycle entrance; a further traversal measures its length. The method uses constant extra space complexity and time proportional to the preperiod plus cycle length.

Maximum subarray problem

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Given a finite sequence of real numbers, find a nonempty contiguous block with maximum sum. Its restriction to contiguous blocks distinguishes it from choosing an arbitrary subset. The problem admits a linear-time solution using Kadane's algorithm.

Kadane's algorithm

Words: 61
Maximum subarray problem OurBigBook.com
For input a1​,…,an​, let Ei​ be the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous block ending at i. The recurrence relation E1​=a1​ and Ei​=max(ai​,Ei−1​+ai​) is exact: an optimal block either starts at i or extends an optimal block ending at i−1. The answer is maxi​Ei​. Keeping only the current Ei​ and best value gives linear time complexity and constant extra space complexity.

Backtracking

Words: 44
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Build a candidate incrementally, abandoning a partial candidate as soon as no valid completion is possible. A depth-first search explores one choice, restores the previous state, and tries the next. Constraint propagation and bounds can greatly reduce the visited state space, although the worst-case time complexity may remain exponential.

Sliding-window algorithm

Words: 50
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
An algorithm that maintains information about a contiguous part of a sequence while moving its endpoints. Updating a fixed-length window sum needs subtraction of the outgoing term and addition of the incoming term. A window product can be updated by division only when the outgoing factor is nonzero; zero counts or zero-free segments handle that exception.

Brute-force search

Algorithm OurBigBook.com
A search algorithm that tests candidates directly, without exploiting enough structure to avoid their enumeration. A small brute-force implementation is often useful for checking an optimized algorithm independently.

Search pruning

Words: 44
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Discarding a branch of a search tree after proving that no completion can satisfy the constraints or improve the current best solution. For minimization, a lower bound on every completion justifies pruning when it is at least the best value already found; this is the principle behind branch and bound.

Number-theoretic sieve

Words: 420 Articles: 11
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
A number-theoretic sieve processes many integers together by marking or updating those sharing a divisor, rather than testing each integer independently. The sieve of Eratosthenes marks composite multiples of successive prime numbers; related sieves accumulate a smallest prime factor, Euler's totient function, or Möbius function for every argument up to a bound. The useful structure is that the multiples of a fixed integer form an arithmetic progression, so one loop can update all affected entries in an array.
For example, initializing an array to true and then marking 2p,3p,… for each surviving prime number p leaves precisely the prime numbers unmarked, apart from the separately excluded zero and one. Every composite number has a prime factor, which proves that every composite is eventually removed. Starting the marking at p2 avoids work already performed by smaller prime numbers. Different sieves use different update rules and time complexity bounds; the name alone does not imply the complexity of the sieve of Eratosthenes.

An odd-only sieve stores only odd candidates, handling the prime two separately. This reduces the candidate storage and avoids marking even composites repeatedly.

Number-theoretic sieve OurBigBook.com
A totient sieve computes the Euler totient function for many integers at once. Initialize ϕ(n)=n and, for each prime p, replace ϕ(n) by ϕ(n)(1−1/p) for every multiple n of p.

Wheel factorization

Words: 56 Articles: 1
Number-theoretic sieve OurBigBook.com
Choose a modulus W that is a product of small primes. Every prime not dividing W must be coprime to W, so a search can restrict candidates to the corresponding residue classes modulo W. For several linear polynomials, discard each residue class in which any required value is divisible by a selected prime. The surviving residue classes can be combined using the Chinese remainder theorem.

Number-theoretic sieve OurBigBook.com
A Du Jiao sieve computes a summatory arithmetic function using a Dirichlet convolution identity and memoization of repeated quotient arguments. For the Mertens function M(n)=∑k≤n​μ(k), the identity ∑d∣k​μ(d)=[k=1] gives M(n)=1−∑i=2n​M(⌊n/i⌋). Grouping equal quotients and precomputing small arguments makes this recurrence relation useful for large inputs.

Linear sieve

Number-theoretic sieve OurBigBook.com
A number-theoretic sieve that visits each composite number exactly once, through its smallest prime factor. Keep a growing list of prime numbers; for each i, generate ip only for stored primes p≤spf(i). Each composite m has a unique representation m=spf(m)(m/spf(m)) admitted by this rule, giving O(N) arithmetic updates up to N.

Matrix-chain multiplication

Words: 909 Articles: 3
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Given a fixed sequence of compatible matrices A1​,…,Am​, choose a binary parenthesization of A1​⋯Am​ that minimizes the number of scalar multiplications in ordinary matrix multiplication. The order of the matrices is fixed: parenthesization changes the grouping, not the operand order. Associativity preserves the product while intermediate matrix dimensions change the cost. The possible binary groupings are counted by the Catalan number Cm−1​ for m≥1.

Matrix-chain cost model

Words: 220
Matrix-chain multiplication OurBigBook.com
For matrix dimensions r×s and s×t, ordinary matrix multiplication computes rt matrix entries, each using s scalar multiplications. Thus its cost is rst scalar multiplications, with rt(s−1) additions if each sum starts from its first term. Here we minimize only the scalar multiplication count, using this dense matrix multiplication rule throughout. The counts describe arithmetic operations, rather than measured elapsed time; matrix multiplication methods that exploit structure or use faster formulas require a different cost rule.
Take matrices A, B, C with matrix dimensions 12×5, 5×40, 40×3. Both groupings produce a 12×3 matrix product, but their intermediate matrix dimensions differ:
(AB)CA(BC)​:12⋅5⋅40+12⋅40⋅3=2400+1440=3840,:5⋅40⋅3+12⋅5⋅3=600+180=780.​
(1)
The second grouping first compresses BC into a 5×3 matrix, avoiding the 12×40 intermediate matrix AB. The saving is 3060 scalar multiplications, although both groupings use exactly two matrix multiplications. This is why counting only matrix multiplication operations hides the interesting choice.
Associativity permits these regroupings in exact arithmetic; commutativity is neither assumed nor generally true for matrix multiplication. Swapping A and B here would even make their matrix product undefined. In floating-point arithmetic, round-off error can make the two groupings yield different computed matrix entries; the cost optimum alone does not guarantee the smallest numerical error.

Matrix-chain dynamic programming (m[i,j])

Words: 360
Matrix-chain multiplication OurBigBook.com
Let Ai​ have matrix dimensions pi−1​×pi​, where p0​,…,pn​ are positive integers. For 1≤i≤j≤n, define m[i,j] as the minimum scalar multiplication cost of the contiguous matrix product Ai​⋯Aj​. The endpoints (i,j) of an integer interval identify a dynamic programming state. A single matrix needs no matrix multiplication, giving the base case m[i,i]=0. At the final matrix multiplication, split after Ak​:
m[i,j]=mini≤k<j​(m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]+pi−1​pk​pj​),i<j.
(2)
The two subproducts have matrix dimensions pi−1​×pk​ and pk​×pj​, regardless of their internal grouping. The recurrence relation adds their optimal costs and the final scalar multiplication cost.[ref]
Why is this optimal substructure? For a chosen final split k, replacing either subproduct's grouping by a cheaper one leaves its matrix dimensions and exact matrix product unchanged, so it decreases the whole cost by the same amount. Therefore an optimal grouping can use optimal groupings on both sides. Conversely, each candidate in the recurrence relation joins two achievable groupings. Mathematical induction on j−i+1, starting with the single-matrix base case, proves that the minimum is achievable and no grouping is cheaper.
There are also overlapping subproblems: while evaluating the different final splits of ABCD, the cases A(BCD) and (ABC)D both request the cost of BC. Recursion without reuse recomputes this answer; memoization or a dynamic programming table stores it once. Fill the table by increasing length j−i+1, so both dependencies are ready. Record an attaining split s[i,j] alongside each cost.[ref]
The dynamic programming table has n(n+1)/2 cost entries. For length ℓ, there are n−ℓ+1 entries and ℓ−1 possible splits, so the exact number of candidate evaluations is
∑ℓ=2n​(n−ℓ+1)(ℓ−1)=6n(n−1)(n+1)​.
(3)
Under the unit-cost assumption that arithmetic operations, comparisons and access to stored costs each take constant time, this gives time complexity O(n3) and space complexity O(n2), using Big O notation. These bounds concern choosing a grouping from the matrix dimensions; they exclude the subsequent matrix multiplication work. If the dimensions or costs require arbitrarily long integers, their arithmetic and storage costs must also be counted.

Matrix-chain split reconstruction (s[i,j])

Words: 270
Matrix-chain multiplication OurBigBook.com
Extend the original example by a matrix D with matrix dimensions 3×15, so (p0​,p1​,p2​,p3​,p4​)=(12,5,40,3,15). The Catalan number C3​=5 counts all possible groupings. Their scalar multiplication costs are
grouping((AB)C)D(A(BC))D(AB)(CD)A((BC)D)A(B(CD))​cost2400+1440+540=4380600+180+540=13202400+1800+7200=11400600+225+900=17251800+3000+900=5700​​
(4)
The optimum is (A(BC))D, with cost 1320. Enumeration makes a useful check here, but dynamic programming reaches the same answer by solving ten integer intervals, including the four single-matrix base cases:
i\j1234​10​224000​37806000​4132082518000​​
(5)
For example, m[2,4]=min{1800+5⋅40⋅15, 600+5⋅3⋅15}=min{4800,825}=825. The three final-split candidates for the full matrix product supply a compact certificate:
k=1k=2k=3​:0+825+12⋅5⋅15=1725,:2400+1800+12⋅40⋅15=11400,:780+0+12⋅3⋅15=1320.​
(6)
The first candidate already uses the better grouping of BCD; the worse A(B(CD)) need not be reconsidered at the top level. This is how optimal substructure lets the table represent all five possibilities with only three final candidates.
Read s[1,4]=3, which separates ABC from D. Then s[1,3]=1 separates A from BC, and s[2,3]=2 separates B from C. This recursion stops at every i=j, returning the corresponding matrix name. Combining the returned expressions recovers (A(BC))D, rather than only its cost. Every recursive call uses a shorter integer interval, establishing algorithm termination; a tied minimum may choose any attaining split. The recovered binary tree has n leaves and n−1 internal nodes, so reconstruction takes O(n) steps. Its attraction is the separation between an enormous family of groupings and a small set of reusable dynamic programming states.

Greedy algorithm

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
A greedy algorithm builds a feasible solution by repeatedly committing to a locally preferred next choice. Each commitment is final: the algorithm does not revisit it when later choices become available. In mathematical optimization, the important question is whether those commitments can still attain the best objective function value.
For example, a shared telescope can accept several observation requests with fixed time slots. In interval scheduling, every completed request counts equally, and overlapping requests cannot both be accepted. Choosing the request that finishes earliest leaves the resource available sooner. The example below turns that intuition into a precise rule, then shows why choosing the earliest start or shortest duration can lose jobs.
Greedy algorithms are attractive because a single pass can replace a search through many candidate subsets. However, "locally best" is only a design proposal. A problem-specific greedy-choice property, often established by an exchange argument, must connect the local decision to the actual objective function. The largest-individual-value rule in the 0-1 knapsack problem fails; Dijkstra's algorithm needs its nonnegative-edge assumptions. A rule's success in one optimization task does not justify it in another.

Greedy-choice property

Words: 180 Articles: 1
Greedy algorithm OurBigBook.com
A greedy-choice property says that some optimal feasible solution contains the locally selected choice. Together with optimal substructure in the remaining instance, it allows repeated commitments. An exchange argument often establishes this property.[ref]
For interval scheduling, a safe first choice need not belong to every optimal feasible solution. When several optima exist, a commitment may exclude one while retaining another. The useful loop invariant is that the accepted prefix can still be extended to an optimum. Merely keeping the accepted intervals compatible proves feasibility, which is a weaker claim.

Exchange argument

Words: 89
Greedy-choice property OurBigBook.com
An exchange argument modifies an optimal feasible solution to include a desired choice while preserving feasibility and not worsening its objective function value. The modification need not strictly improve the optimum; equality suffices.[ref]

Given a finite set of jobs with fixed half-open intervals [si​,fi​), where si​<fi​, choose a subset S of maximum cardinality. Each job occupies one shared resource throughout its interval. A feasible solution has pairwise disjoint intervals: for distinct selected jobs i,j, either fi​≤sj​ or fj​≤si​. Thus a finish and the next start may coincide. Every job has value one; occupied time is not the objective function.[ref]
Consider these six original jobs, with arbitrary time units:
jobsi​fi​​A06​B13​C35​D57​E69​F810​​.
(7)
Job B=[1,3) can be followed immediately by C=[3,5) and D=[5,7). Job A=[0,6) conflicts with all three. Starting the resource earlier is therefore not automatically beneficial: one long commitment can displace several shorter requests.
The earliest-finish greedy algorithm uses a sorting algorithm to put jobs in nondecreasing finish time. Scan that order, accepting the first job and then each job whose start is at least the last accepted finish. Break finish-time ties arbitrarily; an empty input returns the empty set. For these jobs, the order and decisions are
finish orderdecision​Btake​Ctake​Askip​Dtake​Eskip​Ftake​​.
(8)
After B,C, job A starts before the current finish five and is rejected. Accept D; then reject E=[6,9) because six is before seven. Finally accept F=[8,10). The result is S={B,C,D,F}, with cardinality four. Leaving [0,1) idle makes room for more jobs.
By contrast, the earliest-start rule scans A,B,C,D,E,F. It accepts A, skips B,C,D, accepts E, and skips F. Its feasible solution {A,E} contains only two jobs. Here A and E meet at time six and are compatible; E and F overlap on [8,9).
There is also an elementary optimality certificate for this example. The four subsets {A,B}, {C}, {D,E} and {F} form a partition of a set of the jobs. A feasible solution takes at most one job from each group: A,B overlap, as do D,E, and each other group is a singleton. Hence four is an upper bound, attained by {B,C,D,F}. Checking all 26=64 subsets gives a unique optimum of size four: {B,C,D,F}.
The earliest-finish theorem states that this greedy algorithm maximizes job count for every finite instance of interval scheduling. For the exchange argument, let q be the first job in an optimal feasible solution and g an earliest-finishing job. Every later selected job j satisfies
fg​≤fq​≤sj​.
(9)

Why is the algorithm fast? Once sorted, each job is examined once, using only the last accepted finish to decide compatibility. The scan takes O(n) time; comparison sorting algorithms give total time complexity O(nlogn) for n≥2, in Big O notation, assuming constant-cost endpoint comparisons. Already sorted input needs only the O(n) scan.[ref]
The reason the shortcut is correct is stronger than "finishing sooner looks good": the exchange argument preserves every later job of a suitable optimum. This is the problem-specific fact that permits final decisions without exploring all subsets.

Algorithm correctness

Words: 3k Articles: 13
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Partial correctness means that, if the algorithm terminates on a permitted input, its output meets the formal specification. Total correctness additionally requires algorithm termination on every permitted input.
A precondition P describes permitted starting circumstances; a postcondition Q describes the required result. Partial correctness says that starting with P and finishing implies Q. Total correctness also guarantees finishing. A loop invariant supplies the connection between these conditions during repeated steps.[ref]
Correctness is relative to a formal specification. Returning the first entry of an array correctly implements "return the first entry", but fails "return the maximum" on [3,1,4,4,2]. A fast wrong answer does not acquire algorithm correctness from its time complexity. Numerical closeness matters only when the formal specification allows an approximation. Software testing and test coverage provide evidence about selected executions; they do not by themselves establish algorithm correctness for every permitted input.

Partial correctness

Words: 212
Algorithm correctness OurBigBook.com
Partial correctness means that every terminating execution begun in a program state satisfying the precondition P finishes in a program state satisfying the postcondition Q. For a sequential program C, the usual Hoare triple notation is
{P} C {Q}.
(11)
Here the notation expresses partial correctness; it makes no promise that C finishes. The precondition and postcondition describe permitted starting circumstances and required final circumstances, rather than tests performed automatically by the program.[ref]
For a sharp example, take the precondition n=4 and the following sequential program over mathematical integers:
i = 0
s = 0
while i < n:
    i = i
The condition remains true, so execution never reaches the instruction after the loop. Consequently its partial correctness claim holds for the postcondition 2s=n(n+1), and even for the impossible postcondition 0=1: there is no terminating execution with a wrong final result. This is vacuous truth, not evidence that the loop computes a sum. The same program fails total correctness for this permitted input.
The distinction is useful in a proof: first show that an answer, whenever produced, is right; then establish algorithm termination. The summation loop verification supplies both arguments for a loop that actually progresses. Its finite trace illustrates one execution, while its loop invariant covers every permitted input.

Total correctness

Words: 288 Articles: 1
Algorithm correctness OurBigBook.com
Total correctness requires partial correctness and algorithm termination for every program state allowed by the precondition. For a deterministic sequential program, every permitted start must reach a final program state satisfying the postcondition after finitely many steps. Thus an infinite execution can satisfy partial correctness, but refutes total correctness for a permitted start.
In the summation loop verification, the loop invariant establishes the answer conditional on exit, and the loop variant establishes exit. Both parts matter: replacing the body by a step that never returns would defeat total correctness even if every completed iteration preserved the loop invariant. Likewise, a terminating loop with the wrong sum fails partial correctness and therefore fails total correctness.
These obligations depend on the formal specification. A program that rejects every input might correctly implement a rejection service, but does not meet a contract promising a sum for every nonnegative integer. A proof of total correctness also gives no particular physical response-time guarantee: time complexity and the execution environment require their own assumptions.

Algorithm termination

Words: 154
Total correctness OurBigBook.com
Algorithm termination means that execution finishes after finitely many steps on the inputs under consideration. Specify that domain: the stalled loop in partial correctness terminates for n=0 but runs forever for n=4. A successful run on one input does not establish termination on another.
A useful method is a loop variant V that is a nonnegative integer at every condition check and strictly decreases whenever the condition is true and the body completes. Also prove that condition evaluation and each body execution terminate. An infinite run would then give an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers, contradicting their well-founded relation. This establishes algorithm termination without enumerating all executions.
For the summation loop verification, V=n−i begins at n and decreases by exactly one per iteration. The body executes exactly n times, including zero times for n=0. Merely bounding a decreasing measure below is insufficient for real numbers: 1,1/2,1/4,… decreases forever while staying positive. The choice of a well-founded relation supplies the essential progress argument; well-founded progress in recursion applies the same idea to recursive calls.

The precondition requires an integer length n≥1 and exact, terminating integer comparisons and variable assignments. The postcondition for returned value r is
r∈{ai​:0≤i<n}andai​≤r for every 0≤i<n.
(12)

A service accepting empty inputs needs a different formal specification, such as a separate absent result.
This Python implementation makes the variable assignments explicit. Its index arithmetic models exact integer arithmetic; fixed-width implementations additionally need enough index range for n:
def find_max(a):
    n = len(a)
    best = a[0]
    k = 1
    while k < n:
        if a[k] > best:
            best = a[k]
        k = k + 1
    return best
For the original input [3,1,4,4,2], initialization gives k=1 and best=3. Reading a1​=1 keeps 3; reading a2​=4 changes it to 4; reading a3​=4 and a4​=2 keeps 4. At successive condition checks, the pairs (k,best) are (1,3),(2,3),(3,4),(4,4),(5,4). The returned maximum is 4.
At each condition check, use the loop invariant
I:1≤k≤n,best=max{ai​:0≤i<k},
(13)
together with the fact that the input array is unchanged. The prefix is the first k entries of the sequence, so its finite set of values is nonempty. The maximum need not be unique as an occurrence: the invariant concerns its value.
Initialization establishes I: k=1 and best=a0​, the maximum of a one-element set. For preservation, suppose I and k<n hold. Then ak​ is a valid array entry. Either the comparison replaces best with the larger value ak​, or it keeps a value at least ak​. Before increasing k, the resulting value is
max(max{ai​:0≤i<k},ak​)=max{ai​:0≤i<k+1}.
(14)
The variable assignment k←k+1 restores the complete loop invariant. Between the two variable assignments, the old prefix formula may temporarily be false; the loop invariant is required at condition checks, not at every instruction.
At exit, k≥n, while I gives k≤n. Hence k=n, and I gives exactly the required postcondition. This establishes partial correctness. The preservation argument is mathematical induction on the number of completed iterations, covering every permitted integer sequence, rather than just the pictured input.
For algorithm termination, the loop variant V=n−k is a nonnegative integer whenever I holds. If k<n, then V≥1. Every body terminates under the precondition and changes V to V−1. Starting at n−1, it reaches zero after exactly n−1 iterations. For n=1, the initial value is already zero and the body is never entered. Together with partial correctness, this proves total correctness.
Starting best at zero instead of a0​ fails on the original negative input [−7,−3,−3,−8]: it returns zero, which is neither an entry nor the maximum −3. Keeping k=1 forever preserves the correct initial prefix claim but loops forever when n>1; a loop invariant alone does not ensure algorithm termination. Using >= instead of > still returns the same maximum value when entries tie, although a version returning a position would need an explicit tie rule.

Formal verification

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Algorithm correctness OurBigBook.com
Establishing specified properties of a system using formal proofs about a precise model. Formal verification connects an implementation to a formal specification; correctness of the model and its assumptions still matters when applying the result to a physical system.
For a small example, the summation loop verification below starts with executable steps and asks two separate questions: does any returned value satisfy the postcondition, and does execution reach that return? A loop invariant answers the first; a loop variant answers the second. This turns an unbounded family of permitted inputs into a few reusable proof obligations.
The model must specify programming language semantics, including the meaning of variable assignments, comparisons and integer arithmetic. A proof about exact mathematical integers need not describe a machine that wraps on integer overflow. Similarly, a correct formal proof of a weak or mistaken formal specification does not establish the intended behavior. Choosing the right formal specification and relating the model to the implemented system remain substantive tasks.
Software testing examines chosen executions and can expose a counterexample. A formal proof instead justifies a statement throughout its stated model; it does not require executing every permitted input. This makes formal verification valuable when rare boundary cases matter, while software testing can still reveal an incorrect model or misunderstood requirement.
In 1969, Tony Hoare presented rules for variable assignment, composition and iteration in a small programming language. His paper explicitly says those rules do not prove successful termination, and discusses the dependence of arithmetic reasoning on the chosen overflow behavior. These reservations already make the model's scope part of the argument.[ref]

Compute 1+2+⋯+n, the triangular number Tn​, for a nonnegative integer n. The empty sum gives zero when n=0. Use exact mathematical integers and keep the input n unchanged; every comparison and variable assignment is a terminating operation. The original sequential procedure is
require n is an integer and n >= 0
i = 0
s = 0
while i < n:
    i = i + 1
    s = s + i
return s
The order of the two variable assignments matters: the addition uses the newly incremented i. For n=4, the pairs (i,s) at successive condition checks are (0,0),(1,1),(2,3),(3,6),(4,10). At the last check, i<n is false, and the returned sum is 10.

I:i,s∈Z,0≤i≤n,2s=i(i+1),
(15)
and the loop variant V=n−i. The equation says that the accumulator is the triangular number for precisely the processed prefix 1,…,i; the inequalities connect that prefix to the loop's condition.

2s′=2s+2(i+1)=i(i+1)+2(i+1)=(i+1)(i+2)=i′(i′+1).

When the condition is true, V≥1; the terminating body gives V′=n−i′=V−1. Therefore the loop cannot repeat forever. Leaving i unchanged can preserve an initial equation forever without producing any answer. The first change breaks the intended postcondition; the second breaks algorithm termination. A trace can reveal these failures, while the two proof obligations explain them.
The exact-arithmetic assumption has a concrete boundary. In a stipulated unsigned eight-bit model where each addition wraps modulo 256, n=23 fits in the input representation, but its intended triangular number is 276. The stored accumulator instead finishes at 20, so the mathematical postcondition fails. This is integer overflow, and the proof above does not apply to that altered model. Restricting the same implementation to 0≤n≤22 prevents overflow in its stored loop values, since T22​=253; alternatively use a representation supporting the required exact integer arithmetic. The equations in the proof are mathematical statements, not instructions to evaluate products in eight bits.

Loop invariant OurBigBook.com
A decreasing measure used to prove algorithm termination. A nonnegative integer loop variant must strictly decrease after every completed body whose condition was true; the body itself must terminate.[ref]
The prefix maximum correctness example uses V=n−k. It counts unread entries and is independent of whether the new entry changes the maximum. Strict decrease and a lower bound are insufficient for arbitrary real numbers. The positive sequence 1,1/2,1/4,… strictly decreases and is bounded below by zero, but never reaches zero. Choosing an integer measure avoids this failure.

Linear search

Words: 938 Articles: 2
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Linear search, also called sequential search, examines a finite sequence from its beginning, performing an equality test on each entry until one matches the target or the entries run out. It needs no sorted array or total order on the values. This makes it useful for a small collection, a one-off lookup, or data available only in succession: the next entry is enough to make progress.
Specify the answer precisely. For an array A of length n≥0 with indices 0,…,n−1 and target x, return the smallest index j satisfying Aj​=x, or a distinct absent result if no such index exists. Repeated values are allowed. In this contract, finding a later duplicate is insufficient when an earlier match exists. Assume the input remains unchanged during the search and each equality test terminates with a stable truth value expressing the intended matching relation.
Here is an implementation in Python; None represents absence and is distinct from the valid index zero:
def linear_search(entries, target):
    for index, entry in enumerate(entries):
        if entry == target:
            return index
    return None
The official Python sequence method s.index(x) likewise specifies the first occurrence, but signals absence by raising ValueError. An API's absent-result convention belongs to its contract.[ref]
Take the original unsorted array A=[7,4,7,2,9]. For x=7, the first equality test succeeds and returns index 0; the other 7 at index 2 is never inspected. For x=2, the checks against 7,4,7 fail, the check against 2 succeeds, and the answer is index 3 after four equality tests. For absent target x=6, all five equality tests fail and the answer is None. On the empty sequence, there is no entry to inspect: return None with zero equality tests.
Value order never justifies skipping an entry in this algorithm. For x=2, stopping because the first value 7 is larger would give a wrong absent result. Any permutation of the input remains searchable by linear search, although the first matching index and number of equality tests can change. By contrast, binary search uses a total order and the sorted array property to discard whole candidate ranges. Its logarithmic time complexity additionally assumes cheap access to middle entries; a sorted linked list does not acquire constant-cost indexed access merely by being sorted. Sorting for a single query also has a cost, and changes positions relative to the original sequence.

Linear search comparison count (C)

Words: 417
Linear search OurBigBook.com
Count just the equality tests between the target and an entry, excluding loop conditions and index updates. If the first match is at index j, linear search uses exactly C=j+1 equality tests. If the target is absent, it uses exactly C=n. Thus for n≥1 the best successful case costs one equality test, and the worst case costs n, attained by absence or a first match at the last index. For n=0, the sole outcome is absence with C=0.
An expected value needs a specified probability distribution. For n≥1, condition on success, assume the target occurs exactly once, and assume its position J has a uniform distribution on a finite set of indices 0,…,n−1. Then the expected value of the linear search comparison count is
E[C∣success]=n1​∑j=0n−1​(j+1)=2n+1​.
(17)
This is the average of the costs 1,2,…,n under those assumptions, with no assumption that the array is sorted. It is not a universal average for arbitrary queries. For example, with n=5, a unique successful target at index 0 with probability 3/4 and at index 4 with probability 1/4 has expected value (3/4)⋅1+(1/4)⋅5=2, rather than 3.
Duplicates also require care about what is sampled. Choose a position uniformly in [7,4,7,2,9], then search for its value. All queries succeed, but the five possible sampled positions give costs 1,2,1,4,5: both positions holding 7 cause an immediate match at index 0. The expected value is 13/5, not (5+1)/2. Uniformly choosing an occurrence does not uniformly locate the first match.
More generally, let the success probability be p>0 and let qj​ be the conditional probability that the first matching index is j, allowing duplicates. Since ∑j=0n−1​qj​=1, the expected value is
E[C]=p∑j=0n−1​(j+1)qj​+(1−p)n.
(18)
Under the unique, uniformly located successful-target assumptions this becomes p(n+1)/2+(1−p)n. If every query is absent, p=0 and C=n without needing conditional probabilities. When n=0, success is impossible and C=0; the successful-search conditional formula is undefined.
Converting the linear search comparison count to execution time needs a cost model. Under constant-cost equality tests, next-entry access, and loop bookkeeping, worst-case time complexity is O(n) in Big O notation for n≥1, with constant overhead even for the empty sequence. Variable-length entries can make an equality test expensive. On a linked list, advance along its links; repeatedly restarting at the head to obtain the next numeric index adds work that the comparison count does not capture. These are exact operation counts and conditional mathematical averages, not runtime measurements.

Linear search OurBigBook.com
The loop invariant just before inspecting index i is: 0≤i≤n, and no entry at an index k<i matches x. Initially i=0, so there are no earlier entries. A failed equality test extends the excluded region by one position and preserves the loop invariant. A successful equality test at index i establishes a match; the loop invariant establishes that it is the first one. At exhaustion, i=n and every entry has failed, so the absent result is correct. The number n−i of remaining entries decreases after each failed equality test, proving termination for a finite sequence. Together these establish algorithm correctness under the assumptions that the input is stable and each equality test terminates. No step of the argument compares the relative order of values.

Depth-first search

Words: 619 Articles: 1
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Depth-first search is a graph search that follows a branch as far as it can before returning to try the next unexplored branch. Starting at a vertex s of an undirected graph on a finite set of vertices, mark s as discovered. Scan its graph neighbours in a fixed order: for each undiscovered vertex, record the current vertex as its parent in a rooted tree in the discovery tree, mark the new vertex, and explore it immediately using recursion. Return when its adjacency list is exhausted. Discovery marks persist after return, preventing a graph cycle from causing repeated exploration. This branch-and-return rule is the maze exploration described in MIT's notes. [ref]
Use the same unweighted undirected graph as breadth-first search, with vertex set V={A,B,C,D,E,F,G} and edges
E={AB,AC,BD,BE,CE,CF,EG,FG},
(19)
where XY denotes the unordered pair {X,Y}. Visit graph neighbours in lexicographic order of their one-letter labels, starting at A. The discovery order, computed by the diagram's generator, is
A,B,D,E,C,F,G.
(20)
The discovery edges in order are AB,BD,BE,EC,CF,FG. They form a rooted tree spanning the reached vertices, with root of a tree A. The other edges, AC and EG, remain in the original graph but never discover a new vertex. In particular, the graph cycle A,B,E,C,A causes no repeated discovery.
At D there is no undiscovered graph neighbour, so its call returns to B. The next call enters E, then C, then F, then G. Immediately after discovering G, the call stack is A,B,E,C,F,G, with G on top; D is still discovered but its call has finished. The maximum call stack depth is six, although seven vertices are discovered. Following the recorded parent in a rooted tree backwards at each step reconstructs a graph path; here the route from A to G is A,B,E,C,F,G, using five edges. Breadth-first search instead finds A,B,E,G, using three edges. Depth-first search establishes reachability but does not guarantee the fewest edges.
An explicit LIFO stack can replace recursion, but its entries and discovery rule must be specified. To reproduce this exact traversal, store one frame per active vertex, retaining the next position in its adjacency list. Advance the top frame by one graph neighbour; if that vertex is undiscovered, mark it and push its frame immediately; pop an exhausted frame. Pushing all undiscovered graph neighbours at once and marking them on push is a different iterative variant. Even pushing them in reverse lexicographic order does not generally reproduce the parent in a rooted tree relationships above: C would already be marked while processing A, so E could not discover C.
With an adjacency list representation, constant-cost discovery checks and frame operations, and the graph neighbours already ordered, depth-first search has time complexity O(∣V∣+∣E∣) in Big O notation. Each reached vertex is entered once and each incident edge is examined at most twice in an undirected graph; initializing all discovery marks costs O(∣V∣). The call stack has depth at most ∣V∣, since no active vertex repeats. Discovery marks and the recorded parent in a rooted tree for each nonroot vertex also need O(∣V∣) auxiliary space complexity, excluding storage for the graph. Sorting adjacency lists to obtain a chosen order is additional work. [ref]
One start explores only its connected component of a graph. To cover a disconnected graph, start again at every still-undiscovered vertex while keeping all discovery marks; the discovery trees form a forest. Depth-first search is useful for reachability, constructing a spanning tree of a connected graph, and organizing the return steps needed by a depth-first traversal of a tree. For detecting a graph cycle in a simple graph that is an undirected graph, an edge to an already discovered vertex other than the current parent in a rooted tree closes a graph cycle; the immediate return edge to that parent in a rooted tree is not itself a graph cycle.

Memoization

Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Memoization retains a completed function result under a memoization key and returns that result when an equivalent request recurs. For a terminating pure function, repeated evaluation can therefore become lookup rather than repeated work. The benefit is especially striking with recursion and overlapping subproblems: a large tree of calls can refer to a small Directed acyclic graph of distinct answers. The memoization cache contract determines whether reuse is correct; the memoization cache lifetime determines whether an answer is still present when wanted.
Memoization records computed answers, whereas a memory cache retains data from computer memory. A CPU cache hit does not by itself prevent a program from evaluating the same function again. Spreadsheet dependency evaluation adds an explicit mechanism for invalidating affected cached cell values after inputs change; a general memoization table does not discover such changes automatically.
A documented early motivation was to let programs improve their efficiency during execution through rote learning: the abstract of a 1968 paper explicitly proposes such a programming language facility.[ref]

Memoized Fibonacci evaluation (Fn​)

The Fibonacci numbers give an exact example. For a nonnegative integer n, their recurrence relation is
F0​=0,F1​=1,Fn​=Fn−1​+Fn−2​(n≥2).
(21)

Shared dependencies form a Directed acyclic graph because every directed edge goes to a strictly smaller argument. Memoization evaluates a distinct argument on first demand; filling values in increasing argument order is the corresponding bottom-up dynamic programming calculation.[ref]
Use an initially empty hash table memo, shared by every recursive call. Count even the first evaluations of the two base cases, store only completed results, evaluate the left term first, and retain all entries. The following original procedure assumes a nonnegative integer argument:
def cached_fib(n, memo):
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]
    if n < 2:
        value = n
    else:
        value = cached_fib(n - 1, memo) + cached_fib(n - 2, memo)
    memo[n] = value
    return value
Every self-call must pass through the memoization lookup. Wrapping only the outer call while leaving inner calls uncached retains the repeated work. Test membership rather than whether the stored value is nonzero: F0​=0 is a valid completed result.
For cold F5​, the lookup arguments are 5,4,3,2,1,0,1,2,3. The first six are absent; the last three reuse completed answers. Results are stored on return in argument order 1,0,2,3,4,5, with values 1,0,1,2,3,5. Thus there are nine wrapper calls, six body evaluations and four additions. Repeating F5​ with the same table takes one wrapper call and no body evaluation. Requesting F6​ next evaluates only its body, reuses F5​ and F4​, and stores F6​=8: three wrapper calls, one body evaluation and two hits.
The direct-call count satisfies C0​=C1​=1 and Cn​=1+Cn−1​+Cn−2​. Its exact solution is Cn​=2Fn+1​−1, as substitution into this recurrence relation verifies. With the specified memoization procedure, a cold call at n≥2 evaluates n+1 distinct bodies, makes n−1 additions and makes 2n−1 wrapper calls. There are n−2 hits: each of the n−1 nonbase bodies issues two recursive calls, in addition to the initial call. The difference is between the number of occurrences and the number of distinct subproblems.

Recursion (computer science)

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Recursion solves a problem by invoking the same procedure on smaller instances, with base cases answered directly. For merge sort, an empty or one-entry array is already sorted, and every larger array is split into two shorter parts. The decreasing lengths justify termination; a self-call without a progress rule would not suffice.
A recursive procedure refers to itself, directly or through another procedure. A recursive call starts another invocation, with its own arguments and local variables; the caller can wait for its returned output. A base case supplies an answer without further recursive calls. To establish algorithm termination, also show that every recursive call progresses in a well-founded relation. “Smaller” means smaller in that chosen relation: argument values need not all decrease, and the arguments need not even be numbers.
Recursion is especially expressive when a data structure already decomposes into smaller structures. A binary tree has two child subtrees, so structural recursion can follow its shape. A short rule for each case can describe an entire traversal or computation. The distinction between a recursive procedure and the recursive process it generates helps connect that compact description to its resource use.[ref]

The natural number measure n decreases by one on every recursive call, so algorithm termination follows. A divide-and-conquer algorithm divides a problem into smaller instances, solves them using recursion, and combines their answers. In merge sort, the division makes two contiguous halves, and the merge algorithm combines the resulting sorted arrays. The important design step is finding a combination rule cheaper than solving the whole problem afresh.
Halving the input is only one part of the design. The number of recursive calls and the work outside those calls determine whether the smaller instances actually save time. Divide-and-conquer combination cost keeps these quantities separate; the divide-and-conquer product ledger shows how an algebraic identity changes the number of required calls in Karatsuba multiplication.
For algorithm correctness, specify the meaning of each returned answer, prove the base cases, and show that combining correct smaller answers gives the required output. Induction then proves correctness, provided every recursive call progresses towards a base case. The combination rule must reconstruct everything the caller needs: two sorted halves alone are not a sorted array, and four digit blocks alone are not their integer product.

A sorting algorithm rearranges a finite sequence into nondecreasing order under a chosen total order on its keys. Its output must contain every input entry exactly once, including repetitions: producing ordered values is insufficient if entries are lost. Merge sort is one such algorithm; stable sorting adds a requirement about equal keys.
Sorting creates reusable structure: equal sort keys become adjacent, and a sorted array supports binary search. However, an algorithm correctness check must establish both sortedness and sorting permutation preservation. Replacing every entry by the smallest key can produce ordered keys while destroying the original data. Stable sorting imposes a third condition when equal sort keys occur: retain their arrival order.
For example, take complete sorting records (2,A),(1,B),(2,C),(1,D), with the first component as the sort key and the letter as associated data. A correct output is (1,B),(1,D),(2,A),(2,C). The sort keys are ordered, every complete sorting record remains, and the equal-key pairs keep A before C and B before D. The output (1,D),(1,B),(2,C),(2,A) satisfies sortedness and sorting permutation preservation, but fails stable sorting. The output (1,B),(1,B),(2,A),(2,A) has the right multiset of sort keys but loses C,D and duplicates A,B; it fails sorting permutation preservation of complete sorting records.
To express stable sorting precisely, label every input occurrence by its original position, even when two complete sorting records have identical contents. Let p(i) be the output position of the occurrence originally at position i. Besides sortedness and sorting permutation preservation, require
i<j and k(Ai​)=k(Aj​)⟹p(i)<p(j).
(29)
Here k is the sort key function. Sorting by the pair (k(Ai​),i) under lexicographic order gives the same order as stable sorting by k: the original position breaks ties without discarding associated data. For a two-field ordering, first apply stable sorting by the secondary sort key, then apply stable sorting by the primary sort key. The second pass retains the secondary order within each group of equal primary sort keys. For instance, (2,B),(1,C),(2,A),(1,A) first becomes (2,A),(1,A),(2,B),(1,C) by letter, then (1,A),(1,C),(2,A),(2,B) by number.

The loop invariant is that, before pass i, positions 0,…,i−1 satisfy sortedness and contain precisely the entries originally in that prefix. Each leftward step decreases the position, and each completed pass increases the prefix length, so the algorithm terminates.

An already sorted array needs only n−1 key comparisons for n≥1 and no swaps. The adjacent-swap version uses constant auxiliary space complexity. Small or nearly sorted arrays can therefore make insertion sort useful despite its quadratic worst case.

Comparison sort

Words: 332 Articles: 1
Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
A comparison sort learns the ordering of sort keys only by comparing pairs. The keys are otherwise opaque: their numeric values, digits or encodings cannot choose an array index or a branch. It may move complete sorting records and retain previous answers. Merge sort and the adjacent-swap insertion sort are comparison sorts; counting sort and radix sort exploit additional information.

Any deterministic comparison sort correct for all orders of n distinct sort keys needs at least ⌈log2​(n!)⌉ comparisons on some input. Here n! is a factorial, log2​ a logarithm, and the brackets denote the ceiling function. This is a worst-case requirement, not a requirement on every input.[ref]
For three distinct sort keys, the diagram has one leaf for each possible ordering of the original entries a,b,c. Some paths need two comparisons, others three; two comparisons cannot distinguish all six orders.
For the proof outline, represent adaptive comparisons by a binary tree: distinct sort keys give only two outcomes per comparison. A leaf fixes an output permutation; one leaf cannot correctly handle two different strict orders. Hence there must be at least n! leaves. Maximum depth h permits at most 2h leaves, so 2h≥n! gives the bound. Even a three-way comparator has only two reachable outcomes on this distinct-key family.
The growth follows without a precise approximation to the factorial. At least ⌊n/2⌋ of its factors are at least n/2, so for n≥2,
log2​(n!)≥⌊n/2⌋log2​(n/2).
(32)
The brackets denote the floor function. This gives a constant times nlogn lower bound for large n, matching the worst-case comparison growth of merge sort.
Distinct sort keys are essential to the n! counting argument. Identical sort keys do not create n! different strict orders. If all sort keys coincide, stable sorting returns the arrival order. This does not remove the worst-case bound for a comparison sort required to handle arbitrary distinct-key inputs.

Counting sort uses integer sort keys in {0,…,K−1} directly as indices into an array of counts. Constant-cost counting and indexing give O(n+K) time complexity in Big O notation. To retain complete sorting records, cumulative counts locate their output ranges; filling each range from its end while scanning the input backwards gives stable sorting. Emitting bare sort keys from counts would discard associated data. The K term matters when the key range is large.[ref]
For an original worked example, take n=7 complete sorting records and K=4 possible integer sort keys:
A=((2,A),(0,B),(2,C),(1,D),(0,E),(3,F),(2,G)).
(33)

B=((0,B),(0,E),(1,D),(2,A),(2,C),(2,G),(3,F)).
(34)
The equal-sort key groups retain B,E and A,C,G in arrival order. Counting sort prefix ranges explain where those groups belong; stable record placement in counting sort explains how to fill them without losing that order or the complete sorting records.

Sk​=∑h=0k−1​ch​,Pk​=∑h=0k​ch​=Sk​+ck​.

{j∈Z:Sk​≤j<Pk​}=[Sk​,Pk​)∩Z.

For the seven-sorting record example, the frequency array, inclusive cumulative count array, and start array are
c=(2,1,3,1),P=(2,3,6,7),S=(0,2,3,6).

In particular, the three sorting records with sort key two belong at array indices three, four and five. The inclusive cumulative count P2​=6 counts all six sorting records with sort keys at most two; six is the exclusive endpoint, not the final position of a sorting record with sort key two.
These integer intervals fit together because Pk​=Sk+1​ for k<K−1, and PK−1​=n. Their lengths Pk​−Sk​=ck​ add to n, so they partition all output positions without overlaps or gaps. An absent sort key contributes an empty integer interval: with frequencies (0,2,0,1), the endpoints are (0,2,2,3) and sort key two has range [2,2). For empty input, every count and endpoint is zero; every reserved integer interval is empty. This makes the same formulas cover missing sort keys and the empty case.

Stable record placement in counting sort (Ek​←Ek​−1,BEk​​←Ai​)

Words: 725
Counting sort OurBigBook.com
Initialize a mutable endpoint array E to the inclusive cumulative counts P. Scan input array indices i=n−1,n−2,…,0. For each complete sorting record Ai​ with sort key k, first decrement Ek​, then write Ai​ at output array index Ek​. This is equivalent to writing at the old endpoint minus one and then decrementing the endpoint.[ref]
In the worked example, the first input sorting record read is (2,G) at array index six. Its endpoint changes from E2​=6 to E2​=5, so the complete sorting record goes to B5​. Next, (3,F) changes E3​ from seven to six and goes to B6​. Writing before the decrement at the old endpoint would put G outside its reserved integer interval and try to put F beyond the output array. All seven writes are:
step1234567​input index i6543210​Ai​(2,G)(3,F)(0,E)(1,D)(2,C)(0,B)(2,A)​Ek​ before→after6→57→62→13→25→41→04→3​output index5612403​​
(38)
Each endpoint changes only when a sorting record with its own sort key is placed. Consequently, E2​ stays at five through the placements of F,E,D before dropping to four for C.
Here is a complete implementation under the stated input contract; each sorting record is a pair whose first component is its integer sort key:
def counting_sort_records(records, K):
    end = [0] * K
    output = [None] * len(records)
    for key, data in records:
        end[key] += 1
    for key in range(1, K):
        end[key] += end[key - 1]
    for i in range(len(records) - 1, -1, -1):
        key = records[i][0]
        end[key] -= 1
        output[end[key]] = records[i]
    return output
The same array end successively stores frequencies, inclusive cumulative counts, and moving exclusive endpoints; the formulas c,S,P describe their mathematical values without requiring three stored arrays. The write copies the complete sorting record, including its associated data. In particular, two occurrences of an identical pair still cause two separate writes.
For a short algorithm correctness proof, let rk​ be the number of already placed sorting records with sort key k. A loop invariant is
Ek​=Pk​−rk​,[Sk​,Ek​) is unfilled,[Ek​,Pk​) is filled.
(39)
All integer intervals here mean output array indices. Initially rk​=0, so each whole reserved integer interval is unfilled. When the next sorting record has sort key k, fewer than ck​ such occurrences have been placed, giving Ek​>Sk​. Decrementing selects a fresh slot inside its reserved integer interval. At termination, rk​=ck​ and Ek​=Sk​: every output slot has been filled exactly once with a complete input occurrence. The disjoint, increasing sort key ranges establish sortedness, while the fresh-slot property establishes sorting permutation preservation.
For stable sorting, take two input occurrences with equal sort keys at array indices i<j. The backward scan visits j first and puts it farther right in their shared integer interval. When i is visited, the endpoint has decreased at least once, so its output position is smaller. Thus their original order survives. A forward scan with this same decrement rule reverses every equal-sort key group: it would put A,C,G at positions five, four, three. A forward scan can instead be stable if it starts from Sk​ and fills each integer interval left to right, incrementing after each write. The scan direction and endpoint convention must agree.
Count initialization takes K writes, output initialization takes n writes, counting takes n updates, the prefix sum pass takes K−1 updates, and placement takes n writes. Hence time complexity and auxiliary storage are O(n+K) in Big O notation, assuming constant-cost sort key access, integer arithmetic, array indexing and complete sorting record movement. Large records can instead be represented by constant-size references.[ref]
For example, three sorting records with sort keys zero, 999999 and zero require one million counters if K=1000000; unused sort keys still incur initialization and prefix sum work. The bound is therefore linear in the input length only when K=O(n). Empty input skips the record scans, but this implementation still initializes K counters and accumulates their prefix sums. For nonempty input, counting all n records and filling their ranges gives a concrete termination argument.
Direct sort key indexing is a different operation from a binary comparison. The comparison sorting lower bound concerns comparison sorts; counting sort uses its restricted integer sort keys as array indices. Its small-K speed is particularly useful for categorical numerical labels and for each stable sorting pass of radix sort: the reserved integer intervals turn group sizes into exact destinations.

Radix sort (T(n,d,R)=O(d(n+R)))

Radix sort sorts encoded sort keys a digit at a time. Its least-significant-digit version uses stable sorting on each successive digit, often by counting sort. For d digits with R possible values each, it takes O(d(n+R)) time complexity in Big O notation, assuming constant-cost digit extraction and indexing. Stable sorting retains the ordering established by earlier digits when a later digit ties. Both digit access and the direct indexing in counting sort lie outside the comparison sort model, so these bounds do not contradict the comparison sorting lower bound.[ref]

After p passes, 0≤p≤d, the array is in nondecreasing order of sp​(k)=kmodRp, the integer represented by its p lowest numerical digits. Equivalently it is ordered by the tuple (δp−1​(k),…,δ0​(k)) under lexicographic order, with the most significant processed numerical digit first. Among equal suffixes it retains the original order of the complete sorting records.
The loop invariant has a simple mathematical induction proof. Before any pass, s0​(k)=kmod1=0 for every sort key, so the original array satisfies it. Suppose it holds after p passes. The next stable digit sort puts smaller δp​ groups first and preserves the existing sp​ order within each tie. Since
sp+1​(k)=Rpδp​(k)+sp​(k),0≤sp​(k)<Rp,
(43)
the new array is ordered by sp+1​. Equal new suffixes have equal current numerical digits and equal old suffixes, so their original order is also preserved. Stable digit sort

Words: 288

A stable digit sort applies stable sorting to complete sorting records using one specified numerical digit of their encoded sort keys. Counting sort can supply it; stable record placement in counting sort moves records without discarding their associated data. Stability concerns equal current numerical digits, even when the full sort keys differ. This is the information-preservation step in least-significant-digit radix sort.[ref]
An original two-record counterexample exposes the need for the tie rule. Start with (42A​,41B​) at width three. A units pass gives (041B​,042A​). Both tens numerical digits are four. A deliberately unstable tens pass may reverse their tie and return (042A​,041B​): it is sorted by the tens numerical digit, yet its two-position suffixes 42,41 are decreasing. The final stable hundreds pass sees two zeros and keeps this wrong order. Sorting permutation preservation still holds, but sortedness fails. Stability in the tens pass would have retained the units information.
With counting sort as the stable digit sort, each pass initializes R counters, counts n current numerical digits, constructs their prefix sums, and places n complete sorting records. Thus each pass costs O(n+R), and d passes cost O(d(n+R)) in Big O notation. Reuse the counters and two arrays of record references between passes: auxiliary space complexity is O(n+R), rather than O(d(n+R)). Assume constant-cost numerical digit extraction, counter arithmetic, array indexing and record-reference movement; the bound counts these operations, not the cost of copying arbitrarily large payloads or performing arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic.
The benefit is avoiding a counter for every possible whole sort key: width d has Rd possibilities, while each pass needs only R counters. A larger radix reduces the number of passes for a fixed key range but enlarges the counter array. The comparison sorting lower bound does not apply to these direct array indices; they reveal more than a two-way comparison. Nor does fixing R make d disappear: growing key width still increases work.

The positional notation for bounded nonnegative integers has this property. At the most significant differing position m, a one-unit numerical digit difference contributes Rm, while all lower positions together contribute at most
(R−1)∑j=0m−1​Rj=Rm−1.

This geometric series shows why lower numerical digits cannot reverse that comparison. Leading zero padding works here because it preserves place values and the represented integer.
For signed integers in a known integer interval L≤x≤U, encode e(x)=x−L and choose d with U−L<Rd. This order-preserving function is also injective: x<y exactly when e(x)<e(y). For −8≤x≤7, the four-bit encodings of −8,−3,−1,0,4,7 are 0000,0101,0111,1000,1100,1111 after adding eight. Restore the original signed sort keys when displaying the complete sorting records; the encoding need not replace their data. Sorting the unsigned values of raw two's complement bit patterns would put nonnegative integers before negative ones, so their representation alone is not this ordered encoding.
For variable-length strings, first specify the alphabet order and whether a proper prefix precedes its extensions. As an original construction, use a<b, let every string have length at most three, encode a as one and b as two, and append zeros to width three. Zero is reserved for an end marker strictly below every real symbol. The strings ε,a,aa,ab,b encode as 000,100,110,120,200 in radix three, which preserves their lexicographic order. A differing real symbol decides the comparison; at a prefix boundary, the shorter string's zero comes before the extension's one or two. Left padding would instead encode b as 002 and aa as 011, reversing aa<b. Padding raw bytes with zero also fails if zero is an allowed data symbol: distinct strings can then receive the same encoding. A reserved end marker and an explicit symbol ordering are essential; byte order alone does not establish a desired human text order.

Stable sorting preserves the original relative order of entries with equal keys. The entries may carry different names or other information even when their keys coincide. For example, sorting records (2,Ada),(1,Bo),(2,Cy) by the numerical key gives (1,Bo),(2,Ada),(2,Cy): Ada remains before Cy. This is useful when a previous ordering contains information worth retaining, such as arrival order among equally ranked requests.

Sorting algorithm OurBigBook.com
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that sorts a finite array by splitting it into contiguous halves, sorting each half using recursion, and combining the two sorted arrays with the merge algorithm. An empty or one-entry array is returned immediately. For length n≥2, put the first ⌊n/2⌋ entries on the left and the remaining ⌈n/2⌉ on the right; the brackets are the floor function and ceiling function. Always choose the left head on equal keys to obtain stable sorting. This is the split, sort, combine structure taught in the MIT lecture notes.[ref]
Take the concrete input array
A=(7,2a​,5,2b​,9,1,4,3).
(45)
The tags identify the entries originally at indices 1 and 3, counting from zero. Both keys are 2; the tags are never compared. Reading downward in the figure follows the splits, then the returned sorted arrays. Arrows show dependencies; the level layout groups independent calls rather than giving their chronological execution order.
The first two halves are (7,2a​,5,2b​) and (9,1,4,3). Their pairs split into one-entry base cases. Applying the merge algorithm gives the following fully worked return levels; each number in the last column counts only comparisons between two available heads.
Returning levelResulting sorted arraysHead comparisons
Pairs(2a​,7), (2b​,5), (1,9), (3,4)1+1+1+1=4
Halves(2a​,2b​,5,7), (1,3,4,9)3+3=6
Whole array(1,2a​,2b​,3,4,5,7,9)7
In the left-half merge algorithm, the head pairs are (2a​,2b​), (7,2b​) and (7,5); it takes 2a​,2b​,5, then appends 7. In the final merge algorithm, the head pairs are (2a​,1), (2a​,3), (2b​,3), (5,3), (5,4), (5,9) and (7,9). It takes 1,2a​,2b​,3,4,5,7, then appends 9. Thus this precise version makes 4+6+7=17 head comparisons and, ignoring identity tags, returns (1,2,2,3,4,5,7,9).
The elegance of merge sort is that it creates exactly the structure its next step needs: two smaller sorted arrays make the larger ordering inexpensive. Once the whole array is sorted, equal keys are adjacent and binary search can serve repeated queries. Stable sorting also retains information that the keys alone do not express. If the left-half merge algorithm instead takes the right head on the 2a​=2b​ tie, it returns (2b​,2a​,5,7); the keys are sorted but stable sorting has failed.
For time complexity, assume each key comparison, entry access and entry copy has constant cost. The merge algorithm processes n entries in O(n) time. In Big O notation, the resulting recurrence relation is
T(0),T(1)=O(1),T(n)=T(⌊n/2⌋)+T(⌈n/2⌉)+O(n)(n≥2).

The conventional array implementation uses a reusable buffer of n entries for the merge algorithm, together with O(logn) pending calls for recursion. Its auxiliary space complexity is therefore O(n), beyond the original array. This bound describes that implementation. A linked list permits a merge algorithm that reconnects existing nodes; its storage accounting differs from copying array entries into a buffer.

Assuming recursion correctly sorts both shorter halves, the merge algorithm returns all their entries in order. Equal keys within a half keep their relative order by the same argument applied to the smaller call; across halves, every left entry originally preceded every right entry, so taking left first preserves stable sorting. Both half-lengths decrease for n≥2, establishing termination.

Merge algorithm (C(m,n)≤m+n−1(m,n≥1))

Words: 424 Articles: 1
Algorithm OurBigBook.com
The merge algorithm combines two finite sorted sequences under the same total order, retaining every entry exactly once. Keep a position at the first unconsumed entry, or "head", of each input. While both heads exist, compare their keys, append the smaller head to the output, and advance only that head's position. On equality take the left head. Once either sequence is exhausted, append the other remainder without further key comparisons. Empty inputs therefore require no head comparisons. The MIT notes illustrate this two-head combination step.[ref]
For example, the merge algorithm applied to (1,4,7) and (2,3,8,9) returns (1,2,3,4,7,8,9):
The head pairs (1,2), (4,2), (4,3), (4,8) and (7,8) select 1,2,3,4,7 respectively. After the fifth comparison the left sequence is empty, so (8,9) is appended. Seven entries are written, but only five head comparisons occur: tests for exhaustion and appending the remainder are separate operations. This distinction makes the example's count smaller than the bound 3+4−1=6.
For nonempty inputs of lengths m,n, each head comparison consumes exactly one entry. After m+n−1 such removals at most one entry remains, so both heads cannot still exist. Hence the merge algorithm uses at most m+n−1 head comparisons. The bound can be attained: (1,3,5) and (2,4,6,7) require six head comparisons before the left sequence is exhausted. With constant-cost comparisons, access and copying, writing all m+n entries gives time complexity O(m+n) in Big O notation. Writing a separate output array needs m+n entry slots; the two positions require only constant additional storage.
The merge algorithm is useful whenever two already ordered collections must become one: it reads each input only forwards. This works with arrays and linked lists, without needing access to arbitrary middle positions. Choosing left on ties preserves each input's internal order and places equal left entries before equal right entries, which is the combination rule needed for stable sorting in merge sort.
The loop invariant behind algorithm correctness is that the emitted prefix is sorted, contains exactly the consumed entries, and every emitted key is at most every unconsumed key. Each sorted sequence has its smallest remaining key at its head, so the smaller of the two heads is safe to append. The invariant survives each removal; when one sequence ends, the other sorted remainder is safe to append in full. Each comparison removes an entry, so termination follows from the finite input lengths.

Algorithm OurBigBook.com
Binary search finds a target x in a sorted array A by inspecting the middle of the remaining candidate range. If the middle entry is smaller than x, every entry to its left is also too small; if larger, every entry to its right is too large. One comparison therefore rules out many entries. Equal entries are allowed; this version returns any matching index, without promising the first occurrence.
Use indices starting at zero and inclusive endpoints L,R. Initially L=0, R=n−1, where n is the array length. While L≤R, choose
m=L+⌊2R−L​⌋.
(47)
The brackets denote the floor function. Compare Am​ with x: return m on equality; set L=m+1 if Am​<x; otherwise set R=m−1. If L>R, report absence. The updates exclude the already inspected middle entry. This also handles an empty array, whose initial endpoints are 0,−1. Sedgewick and Wayne specify a sorted array as input and return a matching index or −1 for absence.[ref]
For a fully worked example, take the sorted array
A=(2,5,8,12,16,23,38,56,72,91,104,130,160,205,260).
(48)

10…14m=7, A7​=5623<56: retain 0…6.
20…6m=3, A3​=1223>12: retain 4…6.

Returning on equality gives a match; an empty candidate range implies absence. Crucially, this loop invariant allows x to be absent from the beginning.
For a nonempty range of size s=R−L+1, an unsuccessful comparison leaves at most ⌊s/2⌋ candidates. Thus sizes satisfy sk​≤⌊n/2k⌋ after k unsuccessful comparisons. This proves termination and, for n≥1, at most ⌊log2​n⌋+1 middle-entry comparisons. The final singleton still needs inspection: n=1 requires one comparison, not zero. For n=15, the bound is four. This is the halving argument behind logarithmic time complexity.[ref]
A decision tree with q binary tests has at most 2q leaves. Distinguishing n possible matching positions therefore requires q≥⌈log2​n⌉. This lower bound counts binary tests, whereas the bound above counts three-way comparisons.

Karatsuba multiplication is a divide-and-conquer algorithm for multiplication of integers. Splitting each operand into two blocks seems to require four smaller products; the Karatsuba three-product identity recovers the two cross terms together from just three products. Repeating that saving through recursion changes the time complexity from quadratic to O(nlog2​3), where n counts digits in a fixed positional notation. The exponent is about 1.585: the benefit comes from the algorithm, even though each splitting step needs more addition and subtraction.
The Karatsuba worked multiplication below computes 1234⋅5678=7,006,652 using 12⋅56, 34⋅78, and 46⋅134. The original 1962 paper presents a binary numeral system automaton construction: its Theorem 2 and proof reduce multiplication to taking squares of numbers, then reduce a larger square of a number to three smaller squares of numbers. Its footnote explicitly addresses the extra digit in a sum of halves. The sequential time complexity analysis below uses a different operation model from that paper's automaton size and depth bounds, including its Boolean circuit realization without feedback.[ref]
